Submitted by: Maia Hightower, MD, MPH, MBA. Founder, Veritas Healthcare Insights, LLC (DBA: Ask Dr. Maia). Co-author, HAIRA framework (Hussein, Hightower, Beaulieu-Jones, et al., npj Digital Medicine, 2026;9:236). Full comment attached as PDF.

The pilot is timely and the alignment with the NIST AI RMF is the right starting point. Speed is a benefit only when paired with rigorous, real-time monitoring of the populations the products will reach. Comments below use the term "access dimension" to capture the patients most often underrepresented in early-phase trials and in AI training data: uninsured and underinsured patients, rural patients, patients with limited English proficiency, low-AI-literacy patients, and patients in safety-net settings. If the pilot does not engineer for their representation from the start, it will operationalize those gaps at regulatory speed.

Recommendations, organized to FDA's questions:

A.2.b. Reserve at least one-third of pilot slots for sponsors operating in safety-net, rural, and Medicaid-heavy settings. Capability to participate is not the same as prior AI investment.

A.3.c. Patient and investigator representatives should sit on the oversight body in a voting capacity, with representation from underrepresented communities. Their authority should include pre-specified subgroup performance review at each interim milestone, plain-language disclosure for participants, and standing authority to recommend pause when subgroup performance shifts. Investigators should attest annually that they understand the AI tools in use, including the populations represented in training data and known failure modes.

A.6.b. Distinguish behavioral transparency (subgroup performance, drift, failure modes) from architectural transparency (weights, training data composition). Sponsors have legitimate proprietary interest in the latter; they have no comparable interest in the former. Require public posting of subgroup performance reports, drift monitoring summaries, and a one-page plain-language disclosure at each interim milestone.

B.4.c. Require a pre-specified subgroup analysis plan before enrollment. Subgroups should include age, sex, race and ethnicity, primary language, insurance status where collected, rurality, and clinically relevant comorbidity strata. Require site-level performance reporting alongside aggregates. Require generalization testing on at least one external dataset before pilot expansion. Define a performance floor below which subgroup-level results trigger a protocol pause and review.

B.5.a. Operationalize validity through the five HAIRA dimensions: safety, accountability, reliability, equity, transparency. A system strong on three dimensions and silent on two is not validated for clinical trial use.

B.5.c. Specify three audiences and require artifacts for each: full documentation for the regulator, a clinically oriented summary for the investigator, and a one-page plain-language disclosure for the participant, written at a sixth-grade reading level and developed with patient representatives. Comprehension testing on a representative sample is a low-cost addition that materially improves accountability.

B.5.e. Treat fairness as a pre-specified primary endpoint, not a post hoc footnote. Require sponsors to declare which fairness definitions they will use and why, and to report on at least the two most clinically relevant. Require drift monitoring with subgroup specificity. Require consequence specification: what happens when an AI system fails a subgroup performance check should be answered in advance.

B.7.a. Trust is downstream of transparency. Verify what stakeholders know before measuring stakeholder trust, and assess whether trust is distributed across investigator types (academic, community, safety-net) and participant subgroups. Lopsided trust patterns signal that disclosure is reaching some stakeholders better than others.

Broader architecture: Where pre-deployment evidence is incomplete, post-deployment monitoring becomes the load-bearing structure of safety. I encourage FDA to commit, as a pilot deliverable, to a public dashboard summarizing performance across the dimensions above. Representative trial design and rapid AI-enabled review reinforce each other; designing for representation from the start is the faster path to findings that generalize.

Disclosures: Founder, Veritas Healthcare Insights, LLC. Co-author of HAIRA framework cited herein. No financial interest in any company likely to be a sponsor in the proposed pilot.

Reference: Hussein A, Hightower M, Beaulieu-Jones BR, et al. The HAIRA framework: Human-AI reliability assessment for clinical AI systems. npj Digital Medicine. 2026;9:236.

Full PDF version attached for the docket record. See attached file(s)
